extracted.intended_audience: broadband Internet service providers (BIAS providers), ISPs, legal counsel, industry stakeholders, state/local policymakers, and other parties affected by or participating in FCC rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and regulatory standards for classifying broadband Internet access service (BIAS), adopting open Internet (net neutrality) rules, deciding Title II forbearance, and enforcing those rules. Includes bright-line prohibitions, a general conduct standard, transparency obligations, retained authorities, and enforcement mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Broadband Internet Access Service (BIAS) as a Telecommunications Service
rubrics_metrics.description: Reclassify broadband Internet access service (BIAS) as a telecommunications service under Title II of the Communications Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: reclassification enhances the Commission’s ability to fulfill public interest obligations (ensuring Internet openness, defending national security and law enforcement, promoting cybersecurity, safeguarding public safety, monitoring network resiliency/reliability, protecting consumers’ privacy and data security, supporting access to BIAS, improving access for people with disabilities). The order explains how classification accords with statutory text, marketplace reality, Commission and court precedent, and the Commission’s authority to classify services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Mobile BIAS as a Commercial Mobile Service
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify mobile broadband Internet access service (mobile BIAS) as a commercial mobile service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures consumers receive the same protections on mobile as on fixed BIAS and grounds mobile regulation in the appropriate statutory framework (Title III/Commercial Mobile Service authority where applicable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bright-Line Prohibitions: Blocking, Throttling, and Paid Prioritization
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt clear, straightforward bright-line rules prohibiting blocking, throttling, and paid prioritization by BIAS providers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: prevent specific practices harmful to Internet openness. These prohibitions track the 2015 framework and are expected to prevent many harms identified in the record. Bright-line bans operate alongside the general conduct rule to address clearly understood, demonstrable harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Conduct Rule — No-Unreasonable-Interference/Disadvantage Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a no-unreasonable-interference/disadvantage general conduct standard to prohibit deployment of new practices that would harm Internet openness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operates on a case-by-case basis, applying a non-exhaustive list of factors to evaluate whether a BIAS provider policy or practice unreasonably interferes with the ability of consumers or edge providers to select, access, or use BIAS. Designed to evaluate current or future policies not covered by bright-line rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency Rule: Disclosure Requirements and Direct Notification
rubrics_metrics.description: Restore and enhance the transparency rule to require disclosure of certain network practices and performance characteristics and adopt a direct notification requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reverses 2017 changes that eliminated disclosures; transparency supports informed consumer choice. The order specifies disclosure of network management practices, performance characteristics, and terms/conditions of service and adopts a direct notice obligation; small providers may be exempted from some transparency requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Network Management Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow exceptions to bright-line or conduct rules for reasonable network management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits BIAS providers to address legitimate technical needs such as avoiding congestion and combating harmful or illegal content. Practices claimed as network management must meet reasonableness standards; the exception is not a blanket shield for conduct that harms Internet openness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbearance Framework under Section 10 of the Act
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Section 10 forbearance to refrain from applying portions of Title II that are unnecessary to prevent wrongdoing, protect consumers, or otherwise serve the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission balances restoring Title II classification with broad forbearance (e.g., no rate regulation, no tariffing, no unbundling of last-mile facilities, no cost accounting rules) to tailor regulation and avoid unduly chilling investment, while retaining targeted authorities necessary for consumer protection, national security, public safety, and broadband ecosystem preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted Retention of Specific Title II Authorities (Consumer Protection & Competition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain authority under certain Title II provisions (e.g., Sections 201 and 202 and related enforcement provisions) to protect consumers and promote competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintains the Commission’s ability to address anticompetitive conduct and protect consumers; includes enforcement authorities listed across Sections 206, 207, 208, 209, 216, 217, and related provisions necessary for oversight and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement Authorities and Mechanisms (Advisory Opinions, Enforcement Advisories, Investigations, Complaints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a multifaceted enforcement framework including advisory opinions, enforcement advisories, Commission-initiated investigations, and informal and formal complaints to provide clarity and enforce the open Internet rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advisory opinions and advisories offer guidance; investigations and complaint processes provide avenues for enforcement. The framework is intended to provide predictability and flexibility in enforcement responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complaint Process and Enforcement Procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain complaint processes (informal and formal) to hear allegations of violations of open Internet rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The complaint track is part of the Commission’s enforcement toolbox; complaints trigger investigations and potential remedies under retained statutory authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Collection and Reporting for National Security, Public Safety, and Network Resiliency (Sections 218, 219, 220)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain authority to require information collection and reporting to promote national security, public safety, and network resiliency, including outage reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include outage reporting requirements that support coordination with federal partners and defense of critical communications infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customer Privacy and Data Security (Section 222)
rubrics_metrics.description: Restore the Communications Act’s privacy and data security framework governing telecommunications carriers’ protection, use, and disclosure of customer information under Section 222.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restores Commission enforcement and oversight authority over privacy-related practices of BIAS providers; privacy protections are a key rationale for Title II classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to Poles, Ducts, Conduit, and Rights-of-Way (Section 224)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Section 224 authority to regulate rates, terms, and conditions for pole attachments to ensure access is just and reasonable and to support broadband deployment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports deployment by ensuring fair access to critical infrastructure; cited as a benefit of Title II classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal Service Authority and Promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage Title II classification to place the Commission on firmer legal ground to promote universal service goals for broadband deployment and affordability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports programs and policies to expand broadband access in underserved areas and target digital equity objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access for Persons with Disabilities (Sections 225, 255, 251(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure accessible broadband communication for people with disabilities by applying statutory accessibility obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title II classification enhances authority to enforce access requirements and ensure persons with disabilities can communicate using BIAS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Reclassification: What is Included and Excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the scope of reclassification to include Broadband Internet Access Service and to identify excluded services (non-BIAS data services, certain Internet traffic exchange, services furnished to edge providers, and other excluded services).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies boundaries of Title II treatment: what constitutes BIAS, how Internet traffic exchange/interconnection is treated, and which services are explicitly not captured to provide regulatory certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oversight of Internet Traffic Exchange and Interconnection Arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise oversight of BIAS providers’ arrangements for Internet traffic exchange (interconnection/peering) to ensure they do not harm Internet openness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitoring and enforcement can address arrangements that materially disadvantage edge providers or consumers; interconnection-related harms are within scope of oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption of State and Local Regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Preempt state and local broadband regulations that interfere with or are incompatible with the federal regulatory framework established by the Commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reclassification and federal rulemaking provide a mechanism to ensure nationwide uniformity and avoid a patchwork that could undermine Commission objectives; preemption applied where state/local measures ‘may prohibit or have the effect of prohibiting’ provision of a telecommunications service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad Forbearance from Specific Title II Provisions (Enumerated List)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forbear from applying various Title II provisions to BIAS, including (among others) rate regulation (Sections 201/202 as applied to rates), tariffing (Sections 203/204), certain enforcement-related provisions (Sections 205/212), interconnection and market-opening provisions (Sections 251/252/256), subscriber change rules (Section 258), truth-in-billing rules, roaming-related provisions, and terminal equipment rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forbearance is intended to tailor Title II application to modern broadband markets and minimize burdens that could stifle investment, while allowing the Commission to restore essential consumer protections and other authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintaining Certain Non-Title II Authorities (Title III, VI, Other Rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain authority under certain Title III provisions for mobile providers and other non-Title II authorities as necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mobile regulation may rely on Title III and other statutory grants; Commission clarifies retention and forbearance decisions across statutory titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Network Management Standard for Evaluating Practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate asserted network management practices under a reasonableness standard when claimed as exceptions to prohibitions or as part of the general conduct assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include whether the practice is tailored to a legitimate technical need (e.g., congestion management, security), its proportionality, transparency, and whether it unduly harms consumer access or competition. The exception is not a free pass for conduct that disfavors edge providers or consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-Benefit and Investment Impact Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the costs and benefits of reclassification and the specific open Internet rules (Title II reclassification, bright-line rules, general conduct rule, transparency rule, preemption) including potential effects on investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission conducts economic analysis to inform whether rules advance public interest objectives and to weigh potential impacts on broadband deployment and investment; forbearance choices are informed by this analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional Constraints (First and Fifth Amendment Considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure rules comply with constitutional protections, including First Amendment free speech and compelled disclosure doctrines and Fifth Amendment takings analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order considers how rule design and enforcement interact with compelled disclosures, free speech limitations, and takings claims, and frames rules to withstand constitutional review where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of National Security and Public Safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Use restored Title II and other authorities to defend communications networks and critical infrastructure against national security and law enforcement threats and to support public safety communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities may include information collection/reporting, coordination with federal partners, enforcement tools, and rules to improve network resiliency and reliability (e.g., outage reporting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserving Consumer Choice and Competitive Opportunities (Gatekeeper Concerns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Address incentives and abilities of BIAS providers to harm Internet openness and competition by adopting rules that preserve consumer choice and opportunities for edge-provider innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules (bright-line and general conduct) are framed to protect edge-provider innovation and the virtuous cycle linking openness to deployment, competition, and consumer demand.
